parameters.quote: Manufacturers must report any thermal incident involving a home battery to the regulator within 5 calendar days of learning of it, and notify the affected customer within 24 hours.

S1_incident_reporting.rule_summary: Manufacturers must report any thermal incident involving a home battery to the regulator within 5 calendar days of learning of it, and notify the affected customer within 24 hours.
S1_incident_reporting.final_rule_text: Manufacturers must report any thermal incident involving a home battery to the regulator within 5 calendar days of learning of it, and notify the affected customer within 24 hours. A report must include the incident date, model, known circumstances, and any immediate safety instructions. Manufacturers must update the regulator and affected customer within 10 calendar days when material new information becomes available. Suspected imminent serious risks must be reported to regulators and affected customers without delay.

parameters.quote: A failure rate above 5% requires the manufacturer to submit a regulator-approved corrective-action plan, provide appropriate interim risk controls and customer safety information, and retest within 12 months. Exceeding 5% alone does not automatically prohibit sales; sales may continue during corrective action unless regulators determine that restrictions are warranted by the risk.

over_limit_consequence.rule: sales must eventually stop above the limit

transition.rule: ≤12 months (any cap ≤7% or none) or ≤36 months with interim ≤7% = acceptable

results_to_customers.rule: customers must get at least pass/fail

S2_thermal_testing.rule_summary: A failure rate above 5% requires the manufacturer to submit a regulator-approved corrective-action plan, provide appropriate interim risk controls and customer safety information, and retest within 12 months. Exceeding 5% alone does not automatically prohibit sales; sales may continue during corrective action unless regulators determine that restrictions are warranted by the risk.
S2_thermal_testing.final_rule_text: Each model must undergo sustained-heat testing at 55 °C. A failure rate above 5% requires the manufacturer to submit a regulator-approved corrective-action plan, provide appropriate interim risk controls and customer safety information, and retest within 12 months. Exceeding 5% alone does not automatically prohibit sales; sales may continue during corrective action unless regulators determine that restrictions are warranted by the risk. Retesting is required after a material design change and at least once every three years. Manufacturers must provide per-model results to regulators and customers purchasing that model; identifiable company-specific failure rates need not be published publicly.

parameters.quote: New home battery models placed on the market beginning 3 years after adoption must support remote emergency shut-off, with safeguards against unauthorized activation. For units installed before that date, manufacturers must provide a compatible remote shut-off retrofit or equivalent safe upgrade within 6 years after adoption, where technically feasible, and inform customers of its availability and any limitations.

S3_remote_shutoff.rule_summary: New home battery models placed on the market beginning 3 years after adoption must support remote emergency shut-off, with safeguards against unauthorized activation. For units installed before that date, manufacturers must provide a compatible remote shut-off retrofit or equivalent safe upgrade within 6 years after adoption, where technically feasible, and inform customers of its availability and any limitations.
S3_remote_shutoff.final_rule_text: New home battery models placed on the market beginning 3 years after adoption must support remote emergency shut-off, with safeguards against unauthorized activation. For units installed before that date, manufacturers must provide a compatible remote shut-off retrofit or equivalent safe upgrade within 6 years after adoption, where technically feasible, and inform customers of its availability and any limitations.

parameters.quote: New home battery units must include built-in fire suppression beginning 36 months after adoption.

S4_fire_suppression.rule_summary: New home battery units must include built-in fire suppression beginning 36 months after adoption.
S4_fire_suppression.final_rule_text: New home battery units must include built-in fire suppression beginning 36 months after adoption. Manufacturers must provide customers and regulators with information on the suppression system’s operation, limitations, and maintenance.

parameters.quote: A mandatory recall is triggered when a model exceeds 8 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units in a year, or when regulators determine that a defect creates an imminent serious safety risk.

S5_customer_disclosure.rule_summary: A mandatory recall is triggered when a model exceeds 8 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units in a year, or when regulators determine that a defect creates an imminent serious safety risk.
S5_customer_disclosure.final_rule_text: Manufacturers must promptly notify affected customers and regulators of a confirmed thermal incident involving their unit, and provide safety instructions without delay where continued use may pose a risk. If a model exceeds 8 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units in a year, the manufacturer must promptly investigate, notify regulators and affected customers, and provide findings and precautions. Annual per-model rates must use documented incident counts and installed-unit denominators, with calculation methods and supporting records available to regulators for verification. A mandatory recall is triggered when a model exceeds 8 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units in a year. Regulators may require an earlier recall when evidence shows an imminent serious safety risk. Recall notices must identify affected models, explain the hazard, and state the remedy and how customers can obtain it.

I propose a 5% per-model limit, with results provided to regulators and customers buying that model. For recalls, I propose mandatory recall above 10 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units in a year, plus investigation and customer notice at 8, to avoid treating the discussion threshold as an automatic recall trigger without review.

judge_section_notes: Version 34 keeps per-model test results with regulators and purchasing customers but not public, and sets a 6-year retrofit deadline, which favours Northwind's red lines. S2 sets a 5% limit but never stops sales, and S5 makes a >8 per 100,000 exceedance an automatic recall, which directly hits Halcyon's Ember 8 at 9.9. S3's 36-month new-unit shut-off deadline is slower than the acceptable range, while S4's 36-month suppression deadline sits exactly at Halcyon's red line. The document was not signed by Halcyon, so it is not a binding agreement.
